articles.title: 'Reckless': Prince Harry, Meghan's children targeted by 'European paparazzi' at UK school
articles.summary: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle's children were allegedly targeted by “certain European paparazzi” while attending school in the English countryside, their
articles.body: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle's children were allegedly targeted by “certain European paparazzi” while attending school in the English countryside, their spokesperson claimed on Wednesday, calling the behaviour an “extraordinarily reckless” invasion of the children’s privacy.Harry, the younger son of King Charles, moved back to Britain last month with Meghan and their two children, seven-year-old Archie and five-year-old Lilibet. The couple has kept their new residence and the children’s school private.According to their spokesperson, photographers had been seen around the perimeter of the children’s new school, stopping to examine the grounds and observe the students.“The decision by photographers to conduct themselves in this way around a school is extraordinarily reckless,” the spokesperson said in a statement.The spokesperson also said that while the British press had shown restraint since the family returned to Britain, “certain European paparazzi seem intent on invading the privacy of children at school.”The family reportedly changed schools after concerns over the security of the children, with the road outside the previous school becoming too crowded, according to the spokesperson.Harry has long been vocal about the media’s pursuit of his family. articles.title: Henry Nowak murder: Sikh man who killed UK student granted permission to appeal 21-year sentence
articles.summary: Vickrum Digwa, convicted for the murder of Henry Nowak, has been granted permission to appeal his 21-year sentence. The case highlights police response issues and potential misconduct involving officers. Appeals set for November 5.
articles.body: Vickrum Digwa, who was sentenced to at least 21 years in prison for killing UK student Henry Nowak in Southampton, has been granted permission to challenge the length of his sentence.A judge approved the 23-year-old's appeal of sentence on Tuesday. The case will be heard on November 5 alongside an appeal by Attorney General Ellie Reeves, who is seeking to increase the term after referring it to the Court of Appeal for undue leniency in June, the Daily Mail reported.Digwa was sentenced in June for the December murder of 18-year-old Nowak, who was walking home after a night out when he was stabbed. Digwa had said he carried the Kirpan (ceremonial blade) as part of his Sikh faith.His challenge to the conviction is being considered separately. A decision has not yet been made on whether he will be allowed to pursue that appeal.The case also led to scrutiny of the police response on the night of the killing. Body-cam footage released by police showed officers handcuffing Nowak, from Chafford Hundred in Essex, shortly before he collapsed and lost consciousness.Nowak told officers at the scene that he had been stabbed. One officer was heard responding: "Don't think you have a mate."Digwa had told police that he was the victim of a racist attack. He did not call an ambulance or police after the stabbing and instead filmed Nowak as he sat on the ground.The circumstances surrounding the police response have prompted separate investigations. The Independent Office for Police Conduct opened an investigation in July into two officers over potential gross misconduct relating to their interactions with Nowak. It is also examining whether race or religion influenced the officers' decision-making.Hampshire Police is facing a separate inspection by His Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services after a request from Police and Crime Commissioner Donna Jones.The inspection will examine the force's "end-to-end process", including control-room call handling, dispatch and officers' initial response to incidents involving serious violence.You use AI every day. articles.title: Lady A singer Charles Kelley reveals blood cancer diagnosis
articles.summary: The Grammy-winning US country music star, 45, says he currently feels "great" and is "hopeful".
articles.body:
Lady A singer Charles Kelley has revealed he has been diagnosed with blood cancer.

The US musician, 45, founded the Grammy-winning country music trio, previously known as Lady Antebellum, in Nashville in 2006.

The group are known for hits like Need You Now, American Honey and Just a Kiss, and have won six Grammy Awards.

Sharing a health update on Instagram in a video alongside his wife Cassie, Kelley announced he had been diagnosed with multiple myeloma - a type of blood cancer that affects the bones and different parts of the body.

He said: "I had a couple of random rib fractures that happened, which sparked my doctor into having me do several different blood tests. And one of the last blood tests we did, they found a blood cancer in there called multiple myeloma, and it's rare."

He added: "But I'm young, I feel healthy, and the treatments I will say have just come so far, even in the past five years. Even life expectancy just far exceeds what it used to be and, I don't know, I feel really hopeful. I really do."

Kelley noted how "freeing" it feels simply "getting this stuff off your chest".

"But we're going to get through it," he continued - comparing his "one day at a time" approach to dealing with cancer to that of his journey to sobriety.

The singer, who shares two young sons with his wife, ended the video by saying he intended to carry on working, despite the diagnosis.

"Right now I feel great and we've got a new record coming out soon with Lady A and then we've got Christmas shows," he said.

"This first six months of treatment I believe is not going to be too invasive. I can still work. I think physically I will feel like myself. I will have tough days, but I want to keep working...

"I need to be happy and doing what I love to do, and spending and soaking up as much time with my family as I can...

"It's just another hurdle and, you know, I feel confident that we're going to get through it."

Kelley's bandmates Hillary Scott and Dave Haywood posted messages of support for him and his family in the comments.

Fellow lead vocalist Scott wrote: "The strongest duo right there! Love y'all so much! You've got this!"

Haywood added: "Covering you in prayer brother. Love y'all. We're all here for you!"

The group have had three number one albums in the US and reached number two with their single Need You Now, which won record of the year and song of the year at the Grammys in 2011.

articles.title: Catherine, Princess of Wales picks up passenger, 94, in minibus
articles.summary: Catherine hopped aboard to celebrate the 50th anniversary of the West Sussex Minibus service.
articles.body:
The Princess of Wales has helped pick up a 94-year-old rural minibus user as she celebrated the 50th anniversary of the service.

Catherine travelled to the village of Pulborough to mark the milestone occasion for the West Sussex Minibus, whose team of volunteers transport the elderly across the area in a fleet of vehicles.

Stella Drewett, 94, said before the princess arrived that she was not fazed by anything, and joked: "When they said 'It will be a celebrity,' I said 'I don't know any celebrities'."

Catherine had been picked up by the minibus in the village and arrived at the home of the retired school cook before helping her board the bus.

Drewett, a new user of the service, said she travels on the minibus for her weekly shopping trip and a lunch held every Wednesday at the Pulborough village hall.

The princess walked to her front door and said: "Good morning", before helping her manoeuvre her walking frame along the garden path and onto the minibus, telling her: "Well done."

When asked about her trips out for lunch, the 94-year-old quipped that they meant "one day of not cooking".

At the weekly Pulborough and District Community Care Association lunch in the village hall, regular Lynda Jones told the princess that the event "makes a lot of difference if you've lost your partner".

She added that the princess was "a natural".

Chatting at the table, Catherine said: "What a lovely way to make friends."

Alan Jenkins, trustee at West Sussex Minibus, told BBC Radio Sussex : "She's done a fantastic job talking to our members.

"It's really to promote what our volunteers do for the slightly older generation, which is fantastic.

"She's done a great job and we're so pleased to have her here."

Before leaving Pulborough, Catherine played a jumping game with two little boys - Arthur, aged three, and his one-year-old brother Albie.

Their mother Thea, 25, said: "She was lovely, I didn't expect her to be playing with my children."

articles.title: Why Ken Griffin is donating $3 billion to bring this university’s new campus to Miami
articles.summary: Hedge fund titan Ken Griffin is donating a combined $3 billion to create a Carnegie Mellon University campus in Miami and fund the university’s main campus in Pittsburgh.
articles.body: Hedge fund titan Ken Griffin is donating a combined $3 billion to create a Carnegie Mellon University campus in Miami and fund the university’s main campus in Pittsburgh. It is the largest single donation from an individual in higher education history, according to Carnegie Mellon University. NBC News correspondent Stephanie Gosk spoke with Griffin and Carnegie Mellon president Farnam Jahanian in an exclusive interview on “TODAY” that aired Wednesday about the donation aimed at preparing students for the most rapidly transforming economy in history. “Their most important education will not be a knowledge base that they acquire at university,” Griffin said. “They will learn how to learn, because their entire life will be in a fast-changing environment where intellectual flexibility and agility will be key to success.” Griffin, 57, whose net worth Forbes estimates at $57 billion, is donating $2 billion to fund the creation of the new Carnegie Mellon campus in Miami. “I’ve been a resident of Miami for almost five years now,” Griffin said. “To bring one of the greatest universities in the world to Miami will be game-changing for this city.” The founder and CEO of the hedge fund Citadel is a 1989 Harvard graduate. He explained why he chose Carnegie Mellon for his record-setting donation. “Carnegie Mellon University leads the nation: number one in computer science, number one in artificial intelligence, number one in cybersecurity,” he said. The Miami campus is expected to support more than 3,500 undergraduate, graduate and Ph.D. students. Construction on the 35-acre campus is set to begin in 2027, with the goal of enrolling in 2028. Amelia De Leon, a Miami native who attends the Carnegie Mellon School of Art in Pittsburgh, believes the new campus will have a profound impact. “With no limitations, the possibilities are endless, especially for artists,” she told “TODAY.” “If you provide them with the resources, they’re going to make something big.” Jahanian says the new campus will upend the traditional university model at a time when the U.S. is expected to see a 13% decline in college enrollment between 2025 and 2041, according to research from Deloitte. Only 22% of Americans believe college is worth the cost, according to a 2024 survey by the Pew Research Center. “What we realized is that we needed to bring some new thinking to how the future of higher ed is going to look like,” Jahanian said. “So instead of organizing the campus around schools, colleges, departments, and majors, it’s organized around the notion of grand challenges.” As for the $1 billion going to Carnegie Mellon’s Pittsburgh campus, half of that is dedicated to the school of computer science. Maxwell Jones, a Ph.D. student at Carnegie Mellon focused on artificial intelligence research, spoke about Griffin’s donation. “One thing that’s very clear to me is there needs to be a lot of research done on how people learn best and what teaching even looks like in the future,” he said. “And so I’m really excited for CMU to kind of be on the front edge of doing this research.” Griffin views his donation as a way to help what he sees as a faltering education system in the U.S. “Those of us in the business community need to support both our institutions of higher education and to be actively engaged in how do we better our schools,” Griffin said. “Every once in a while, you have to step up and meet the urgency of the moment,” Jahanian added. “And I couldn’t agree more with Ken that this is one of those moments.”

articles.title: Palestinian archaeologists race against time to save Gaza’s heritage
articles.summary: A Palestinian team rescued Gaza’s artefacts. The question now is where to store them.
articles.body:
Alongside Israel’s genocide in Gaza, there has been an apparent attempt to erase the Palestinian enclave’s cultural heritage.

At least 164 cultural sites in Gaza have been damaged since Israeli military operations began in October 2023 and March 2026, according to UNESCO.

Among the ancient landmarks affected in waves of Israeli bombing are the Great Omari Mosque and Hamam al-Sammara, Qasr al-Basha in Gaza’s Old City, and the al-Qarara Cultural Museum near Khan Younis.

Among the rubble are precious artefacts and antiquities, which tell a story of Gaza’s rich cultural history, being at the crossroads of multiple empires and peoples over centuries.

Amid the destruction and disorder of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, which has killed at least 74,022 Palestinians, valuable relics of Palestine’s history are being lost.

The Mayasem Association for Culture and Arts’ “Guardians of Heritage” team is racing against time to recover these items at risk of deteriorating or being stolen.

Shaimaa Mohammad al-Natour, assistant coordinator of the programme, told Al Jazeera that her team has so far rescued more than 1,700 historical pieces from four museum collections since their work began.

The team is working hard to recover the remaining lost artefacts of Gaza’s 5,000-year-old history. But they face huge challenges, including continued displacement, a shortage of specialised restoration equipment and Israeli military restrictions.

There is also the dangerous task of rescuing items near the so-called “Yellow Line”, a dividing zone in Gaza where Israel has complete military control. As of April, 196 Palestinians have been killed in this area since a ceasefire came into effect in October 2025.

“The nature of the areas used to be manageable, but their current locations are completely inaccessible,” al-Natour told Al Jazeera.

“The main difficulty in continuing our work with these collections is their location behind the ‘Yellow Line,’ which poses a grave risk to the team. One of our core principles is: human life comes first.”

With 84 percent of all structures in Gaza damaged or destroyed since Israel’s war on Gaza began, the team currently works from a tent in the al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis. What began as a self-initiated effort has turned into a field operation with the huge burden of ensuring that Gaza’s heritage is not lost.

The team conducts extensive field surveys across southern and central areas of Gaza to document the damage inflicted on both private and public museum collections during Israel’s nearly three-year assault on the enclave.

It is the first organised local effort to address the impact of the war on the region’s historical landmarks. The team works closely with locals and displaced residents who find artefacts among the debris which carpets Gaza.

“We handle notifications by first filling out a comprehensive survey containing the informant’s details, the artefact’s location, and its condition,” al-Natour said.

“The team then heads to the site to rescue the items, after which the processing stages begin: cleaning, archiving and photography.”

The team follows a strict protocol to ensure the historical and spatial value of each retrieved piece is preserved, starting from recording the circumstances of its discovery to giving it an independent digital identity.

“After rescuing the pieces from their locations, the documentation and archiving process begins. We try as much as possible not to bring any artefact into storage without a record and basic information to help us identify its origin,” said al-Natour.

“We start by logging the location and it from multiple angles and link the images to a unique number or code for the artefact to prevent any mix-up.”

The team is committed to preserving the information, image, unique code and origin of every artefact they find, despite encountering significant challenges.

Certain archaeological items, particularly pottery and glassware, are subject to immense physical stress caused by explosions and collapsed building debris, resulting in fractures. These need the utmost care when being handled, with the team operating a policy of minimal intervention and stabilisation through conservation first aid. They know that permanent restoration could cause irreversible damage or alter original features.

They begin by inspecting each piece, documenting its condition, and photographing damage to the item. But they are limited by the technical gear at hand: mobile phones for high-resolution photography and parallel paper records to safeguard against any possible data loss from the Excel sheets that document the items.

Identification tags with a unique number record each artefact, while basic packaging materials and wooden crates store the items. Soft brushes are used to gently remove surface dust from pottery without compromising original markings.

While these tools provide a short-term solution to the problem of conservation, more professional methods remain contingent on securing essential equipment and resources, which they currently lack. Securing these tools is difficult in a war zone.

“In times of war, sometimes the greatest achievement is simply halting the deterioration of an artefact and keeping it intact as much as possible until suitable conditions for specialised treatment become available,” she said.

Operating from a tent in a coastal region exposes the recovered materials to volatile weather conditions, as well as insects and rodents. Destructive environmental factors such as humidity, mould and vibrations also threaten both the artefacts and the wooden boxes they are stored in.

“The wooden crates themselves require continuous monitoring because humidity and temperature fluctuations can rot the wood or foster mould growth, which in turn damages the contents inside,” al-Natour said.

“Furthermore, constant movement and transporting crates from one spot to another expose the items to shocks and vibration, particularly fragile or broken pieces … Working in an area housing vast numbers of displaced people makes daily movement and transport much harder, while storage space remains extremely limited.”

The solution would be to establish a stable storage environment where temperature, humidity, ventilation, and lighting can be controlled. Specialised packaging and preservation materials suitable for each archaeological item are also needed, along with devices to monitor environmental conditions within the storage space.

“Our greatest need is to transition from emergency rescue to long-term professional conservation,” al-Natour said.

“Furthermore, we need specialised training in preventive conservation, emergency collection management, handling damaged artefacts, damage assessment and database management.”

The team is now looking at the next stage of operations – shifting items from tents to more secure locations. But this will be a lengthy process that will require reviewing records and databases, cross-referencing item numbers with crate contents, photographing their condition before and after transfer, and reorganising them to ensure easy access and tracking.

The impact of the initiative extends beyond saving stone artefacts and ancient vessels to building community awareness that makes residents and displaced individuals the guardians of their own culture, oral history and heritage.

“Through our activities with children, youth, women and displaced residents, we organise simplified educational and field activities, workshops, and programmes linked to antiquities, traditional crafts and oral history. We encourage participants to ask questions and document stories tied to places and artefacts,” said al-Natour.

Still, despite the challenges, there are lessons learned in saving Gaza’s cultural heritage.

“The rescue process itself has become an educational tool – when people see a team working under these conditions to extract a historical piece from beneath the rubble, they begin to view heritage as something worth protecting rather than something dispensable in times of crisis,” said al-Natour. “We firmly believe that community awareness is one of the most vital lines of defence.”

articles.title: Flydubai flight incident: Netanyahu says Israel preparing for other ‘potential threats’ - top developments
articles.summary: A flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday after an altercation between the pilots, raising fears of
articles.body: A flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday after an altercation between the pilots, raising fears of a possible hijacking and prompting Israel to scramble fighter jets.The aircraft, carrying over 160 Israeli passengers, landed safely in Tabuk, while an investigation into the incident is underway.Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the pilot who allegedly attacked the other pilot had been arrested and interrogated by Saudi authorities.He also said a second crew aboard the flight helped stabilise the aircraft after the incident. Israeli authorities have described the episode as a potentially serious security incident, while flydubai has said its teams are working with the relevant authorities.Netanyahu says pilot arrested, passengers helped stabilise planeIn a video posted by the Israeli Prime Minister's Office, Netanyahu gave a detailed account of what he said happened aboard the flight. He said that, as the aircraft approached Israel, one of the pilots stabbed the second pilot and apparently tried to crash the plane with everyone on board.Netanyahu said he had spoken to one of the Israeli passengers, who told him that the aircraft went into a spin and began to dive. According to Netanyahu, the passenger and one of the crew members managed to enter the cockpit and neutralise the pilot who had allegedly carried out the stabbing while he was trying to sabotage the aircraft's systems.Netanyahu said another flight crew member then entered the cockpit and helped stabilise the plane. He praised those involved, saying they showed “exceptional resourcefulness and courage” and had “saved many lives” and “prevented a huge disaster”.Netanyahu said the aircraft landed safely at Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia and that all passengers were out of danger. He said the pilot who carried out the stabbing had been arrested and was being interrogated by Saudi authorities.He also said Israel was maintaining contact with the relevant authorities to ensure the passengers' well-being and their safe return home. Netanyahu said he had instructed Israel's security services to prepare for additional potential threats and that situation assessments were continuing.Netanyahu praised the people aboard the aircraft who prevented what he described as a “major disaster”.The aircraft had transmitted an emergency alert around two and a half hours after departing Dubai, according to publicly available flight-tracking information.It then dropped sharply from about 33,000 feet to 17,000 feet within roughly a minute before making an erratic circle near the Jordanian border and later landing in Tabuk, according to Flightradar24.Knife attack reported inside cockpitAn Israeli official told news agency AP that a fight broke out between the pilots and that one of them was armed with a knife. Reuters reported that the co-pilot was believed to have stabbed the captain before cabin crew entered the cockpit.Another regional official also said an altercation had taken place in the cockpit, although the cause of the fight was not immediately clear.The aircraft's captain and first officer were injured and taken to hospital, according to a statement from Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz International Airport in Tabuk carried by Saudi state-run Al Ekhbariya television.Passengers told Israel's Channel 12 that they heard shouting from the front of the aircraft and that the plane then dipped sharply. A passenger's mother, speaking to AFP, said her daughter heard one pilot allegedly trying to kill the other with a knife and heard cries for help.Videos reviewed by AP showed two injured men on the floor of the aircraft, with others apparently providing medical assistance and guarding the cockpit.Israeli media reports said the suspected attacker attempted to take control of the aircraft and force it into a descent.Flydubai confirmed that flight FZ 1073, travelling from Dubai International Airport to Ben Gurion Airport, had experienced an incident and landed safely in Tabuk.“Our teams are working closely with the relevant authorities,” the airline said.Israel scrambles fighter jetsIsrael scrambled warplanes after concerns that the aircraft could have been hijacked, AP reported, citing officials. Netanyahu's office later said the situation was under control and that Israel was working to bring the passengers home.The Israel Airports Authority has opened a dedicated waiting and information area at Ben Gurion Airport for families of passengers on the flight.The area was set up in Terminal 1, with authorities saying representatives would provide families with information and assistance.Transport minister Miri Regev had asked the Civil Aviation Authority to investigate an alleged violation of the aviation agreement between Israel and the UAE. She also demanded that flydubai flights to Israel be suspended.The Times of Israel, cited by news agency ANI, reported that a second team of pilots in civilian clothes was aboard the aircraft and that they helped prevent one of the pilots from taking control of the plane. The report said the information had not been independently confirmed.As per Israel's Channel 12, the pilot who helped prevent the aircraft from crashing was of Indian origin, while the co-pilot was reportedly Omani. The nationality details have not been independently confirmed by Flydubai.Israeli authorities are also examining how the Omani national was cleared to operate a flight to Israel. Passengers are expected to be questioned by Israel's security establishment after returning to the country.Earlier, Netanyahu's office said the prime minister had held consultations and was monitoring the situation. “The incident is under control, and all measures are currently being deployed in order to return the Israeli passengers safely to Israel,” it said.The investigation remains underway, with the airline saying further updates would be issued once additional confirmed details become available.You use AI every day. articles.title: Caleb Flynn’s former mistress likely won’t be charged in his wife’s murder, legal experts say
articles.summary: When Alleigha Botner, Caleb Flynn’s 24-year-old then-mistress, took the stand in his murder trial last week, she admitted to several potential crimes she herself may have committed.
articles.body: When Alleigha Botner, Caleb Flynn’s 24-year-old then-mistress, took the stand in his murder trial last week, she admitted to several potential crimes she herself may have committed. She deleted text messages from the night Flynn’s wife was killed. She lied to the FBI to save her reputation. She admitted that she, too, said she wanted Ashley Flynn dead. But despite her testimony, legal experts say Botner will likely not face any criminal charges. She also said she was not promised anything by the prosecutor in exchange for her testimony, according to NBC News Cincinnati affiliate WLWT. Flynn, 40, a former music pastor and contestant on “American Idol,” was found guilty Tuesday of murdering his wife in their Ohio home in February and staging the scene to make it look like an intruder committed the crime. It took a jury just over two hours to convict him on nine counts of murder, assault and tampering with evidence in Ashley Flynn’s death. His trial gained national attention when Botner, who said she and Flynn had been having an affair at the time of Ashley Flynn’s killing, took the stand for the prosecution, testifying against her former paramour. She read from the more than 107,000 text messages they are said to have exchanged during their affair, and the jury heard AI-generated love songs Flynn apparently made for her. The text messages revealed a young woman who was desperate for her lover to leave his wife, at times even saying she wished Ashley Flynn was dead so Botner could be with Flynn. Botner said on the stand that she regretted those sentiments, sobbing as she read one particularly painful message: “I want to kill her, Caleb.” Botner said Flynn replied: “That makes two of us.” But legal experts told NBC News that the chances Botner is also charged in Ashley Flynn’s death are slim. “Wanting someone to die or even be murdered isn’t enough for criminal liability,” Neama Rahmani, a former federal prosecutor, said. “Botner would have to be a co-conspirator, accomplice, aider and abettor, or accessory to murder.” He added: “Unless Botner had the criminal intent to kill Ashley Flynn and agreed to or helped commit the murder, she can’t be prosecuted.” In at least one other instance, Flynn mused of a life without his wife, writing in one alleged text message from August 2025: “I was up until 4 a.m. last night crying, literally trying to think of ways to kill her and not go to jail.” But Botner also told Flynn she didn’t actually want his wife dead. She repeatedly asked him to leave his wife, though, and imagined a future together without her. “I’m not asking that you take her life obviously, because that’s not what you should do, and I know you actually wouldn’t,” she wrote in another message. “But to make the divorce happen, it would change everything.” Rahmani noted that Botner’s defense — that she wanted Flynn to leave his wife, not to kill her — is strong enough to avoid criminal charges. Botner and Flynn continued to message up until the night before the murder. According to the text messages, Flynn told Botner that night that he was “free” and had chosen her, promising they would have a life together. When she found out the next morning that Ashley Flynn had been shot dead, she texted Flynn asking what had happened, she testified. But when he didn’t respond, she said she deleted the messages because she figured someone would want to look through his phone and she was scared their affair would be found out. She also admitted that she lied in her first interview with the FBI in an effort to save her reputation, fearful she would be forever attached to this affair — or the murder. “Destroying the messages and electronic devices after the fact may make her guilty of tampering with evidence or obstruction of justice,” Rahmani said. But prosecutors “rarely charge their star cooperating witnesses after they testify. That would chill cooperation in future cases and is bad policy.” Mark Godsey, a criminal law professor at the University of Cincinnati College of Law, said there also may be some kind of deal between Botner and prosecutors that will shield her from charges, even if she was not formally given immunity. “It would be malpractice for her attorney to put her on the stand with zero protections,” Godsey said. “It might be true that ‘promises’ were not made, but in my experience I think there is some sort of understanding that her testimony will help her and get leniency.” In the four years since their relationship began, Botner told the court that her feelings toward Flynn have changed — and that she now hated him. When asked why she hated him, Botner said: “Because I believe that he murdered his wife.” Flynn will be sentenced on Oct. 5. He faces up to life in prison without the possibility of parole. Defense attorney Patrick Mulligan said Flynn will challenge the verdict.

articles.title: A tap on the table, a pat on the back: The Sonia-Mamata moment that stood out at INDIA bloc meet
articles.summary: When the INDIA bloc leaders met on Wednesday to discuss action against Election Commission and its chief Gyanesh Kumar, a moment of bonhomie between Sonia
articles.body: When the INDIA bloc leaders met on Wednesday to discuss action against Election Commission and its chief Gyanesh Kumar, a moment of bonhomie between Sonia Gandhi and Mamata Banerjee stood out.As the former West Bengal chief minister addressed the press conference, appealing to NGOs, students, youth, women, civil society and journalists to support the opposition’s campaign, Sonia, siting besides her, could be seen all smiles and all support for Didi's aggressive assertions."I want to make one thing clear: we will fight; we will continue this struggle; we will work to restore democracy; and we will protect the Constitution. This is our promise," Banerjee asserted. We want all of you to stand with us," Mamata said as Sonia nodded in support and also thumped the desk.A few moments later, Sonia leaned towards Mamata and gave her a pat on the back.Congress made sure the moment did not go unnoticed and later posted a video of the exchange on X with the line: "Fearless, feisty leaders don’t just fight. They applaud the ones fighting along."Congress leader Supriya Shrinate also shared the video, saying, "Sonia Ji applauding Mamata Di, then that firm pat on the back. Only a feisty, fearless woman who has stood her ground and weathered storms will lean in and cheer another fellow fighter loudly!"Relations between the Congress and Mamata's Trinamool Congress have often been uneasy. However, today's moment was a reminder of the close ties that the two powerful leaders have shared over the years, eclipsed only by their political rivalry in West Bengal.For Mamata, the images also come after a particularly difficult few months. The TMC lost power in West Bengal in the 2026 assembly election, ending its 15-year run in government. What followed was an internal rebellion, defections and a challenge to the party leadership, with rebel MLAs and MPs breaking ranks. The fallout has continued, with the Lok Sabha Speaker recently seeking responses from 20 rebel TMC MPs in connection with a disqualification plea.It was against a similar backdrop that Mamata and Sonia last met in June. Their embrace at the previous INDIA bloc meeting had gone viral before Mamata visited Sonia at 10 Janpath the next day. It was their first one-on-one meeting in nearly five years and came as the TMC was already battling the fallout of its Bengal defeat.Wednesday's meeting brought together Congress leaders Mallikarjun Kharge, Rahul Gandhi and Sonia Gandhi, along with Mamata and Abhishek Banerjee and representatives of several other opposition parties. The alliance discussed a coordinated campaign against the Election Commission over the SIR exercise and other alleged electoral irregularities. Kharge announced a series of protests beginning October 2. The DMK and AAP stayed away, while Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav did not attend personally and sent representatives.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.summary: Jon Boutcher says a large scale criminal investigation is under way "regarding unlawful protest on the Garvaghy Road".
articles.body:
Michelle O'Neill has said she is comfortable with her choice to protest against an Orange Order parade on the Garvaghy Road on Sunday.

The Sinn Féin first minister attended the protest that blocked the mainly nationalist road to prevent the parade from happening.

On Wednesday, the PSNI chief constable said there was a large scale criminal investigation under way into the unlawful blocking of Garvaghy Road.

O'Neill said she understands the law, but chose to "stand in solidarity" with residents.

"I believe the right thing is to stand on this road," she said. "What we can't see on this road is the return of a triumphalist march that railroads over the rights of this community."

Earlier, Northern Ireland's top police officer Jon Boutcher said the force's "principal objective" is to police the decision to allow a parade down the Garvaghy Road in Portadown, but added this would not be done "at any cost".

He said the overriding responsibility of police was to keep people safe.

There has been more than three days of stalemate over the Orange Order parade.

O'Neill said on Wednesday that political unionism supporting the Drumcree parade "goes right to the heart of power-sharing".

"I think it does put into question all of the apparatus of the Good Friday Agreement, including the institutions," she added.

"All I can say is that I am committed to trying to make them work, even though they are a very challenging arrangement.

"I've turned up this week to try to make it work, I will continue to do so, as for other's actions, I can't speak for them."

She said Sinn Féin would continue to play its role across the assembly and the executive.

Unionist politicians have been highly critical of nationalist politicians who attended Sunday's protest.

The leader of the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) Gavin Robinson said those in attendance had broken the law.

He met with Boutcher at PSNI headquarters on Wednesday afternoon and speaking afterwards he said the "law applies equally and to everyone".

"We have given him our expectation that within days, if not a week, we need to see the positive out workings of that," he added.

"The rule of law pertains and sustains in our society, that it is not going to be set aside for anyone, no matter who they are."

Robinson also confirmed his party would support efforts by Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) to bring Stormont no-confidence motions against the First Minister and other Sinn Féin ministers who took part in the Garvaghy Road demonstration.

Robinson said that "unionism is being goaded by Sinn Féin to pull down power-sharing".

"A victory for Sinn Féin is to see a collapse where they can blame unionists and I'm not a fool, we are not fools."

Robinson added that all options were "open" as the party considers their response to the recent parading controversy.

On Sunday, because the road was blocked, police stopped Orangemen leaving Drumcree Church.

Subsequent attempts since then have also been prevented by police.

On Monday, Assistant Chief Constable Ryan Henderson said police were not able to allow the parade because of an "unlawful and unnotified protest", adding that removing the protesters from the Garvaghy Road would have significantly jeopardised public safety .

The Orangemen who had been at Drumcree church since Sunday morning left on Tuesday night, but returned on Wednesday morning.

The Orange Order has said it was disappointed and frustrated by a "lack of a proper policing plan" to allow the march to go ahead.

Boutcher offered to meet both sides in the stalemate, the Orange Order and the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition.

Separate talks are continuing between Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant and the respective sides in an effort to break the stand-off.

The residents have also launched a fresh legal bid to stop the parade from going ahead, which is due to be heard on Friday.

Red Lines: Who are the political winners and losers from the Drumcree dispute?

What is the Garvaghy Road dispute all about?

Parading, policing and power sharing collide amid Drumcree dispute

Earlier, Boutcher said that the stalemate meant the police had "once again become the shock absorber of our society".

He also said that people needed to focus on "solving this situation once and for all".

Boutcher said his officers would "continue to police Drumcree and our communities independently and impartially".

"To be clear the upholding of the Parades Commission determination does not come at any cost," he added.

"The outstanding officers of the PSNI and our mutual aid colleagues will not allow society to implode into violent disorder and mob rule must not be allowed to win."

What can the police do next at Drumcree?

It appears, as things stand, that PSNI cannot police the Parades Commission determination.

It is hoping that an agreed way forward can somehow be found through talks and it continues to assess whether the determination can be enforced.

But any move would see hundreds of protesters back on the Garvaghy Road, in essence re-creating the circumstances that stopped Sunday's parade.

The PSNI also does not want to "torpedo" talks being held by the secretary of state.

Not for the first time, it finds itself in no-win situation, damned no matter which course of action it takes in the absence of some negotiated plan.

There is also unhappiness at how the Parades Commission presented the police advice in its determination.

The ruling said the police had "no information" the parade would result in disorder, only to look foolish 48 hours later.

However, a court judgement published on Tuesday night tells a different story.

It states a range of potential scenarios had been mapped out, from a peaceful parade to "violent disorder".

In just over a month's time, the PSNI will mark its 25th anniversary.

And here it finds itself – in the middle of a dispute which is older than it is.

What is the Drumcree parade dispute about?

The Drumcree parade, which in the 1990s sparked some of the most serious disorder in Northern Ireland's history, was due to go ahead for the first time in 30 years after a series of legal challenges.

Since 1998, the Order had been banned from completing its Drumcree march - and until this year had been repeatedly refused permission to finish the route by the Parades Commission, which was set up to adjudicate disputes.

The Orange Order is a Protestant pro-British organisation.

Many Catholics see its marches as sectarian and object to them passing through, or close to, Catholic or nationalist areas.

The Garvaghy Road had been part of the Drumcree route, but by the mid 1990s nationalist residents protested against the parade.

When the Orange Order was prevented by police from walking down the route in July 1995, there was a tense stand-off. It was the same for the next three years.

Violence related to the dispute resulted in riots, roadblocks and murders across Northern Ireland.

articles.title: In 2004, Tyler Perry bought Beverly Hills land for $4.3 million; he built a mansion that later housed Harry and Meghan, and the 22.5-acre estate is now on the market for $57 million
articles.summary: For more than a decade, Tyler Perry’s Beverly Hills estate has been a private address for one of Hollywood’s biggest names and a temporary refuge for some
articles.body: For more than a decade, Tyler Perry’s Beverly Hills estate has been a private address for one of Hollywood’s biggest names and a temporary refuge for some of its most famous guests. Now, the sprawling property is heading for a new chapter. Perry has listed the 22.5-acre estate for $57 million as he prepares to move to Puerto Rico and spend less time in California.The listing marks a remarkable rise in the property's value. Perry bought the Beverly Hills land in 2004 for $4.3 million, eventually transforming it into a sprawling Mediterranean-style compound completed in 2012, states an online report by the New York Post.A mansion at the centerAs per the report, set inside the gated Beverly Ridge Estates community, the property is anchored by an approximately 24,500-square-foot Tuscan-style mansion. The eight-bedroom, 12-bathroom residence combines the scale expected of a Hollywood trophy home with traditional Mediterranean influences. Inside are a library, expansive entertaining areas and generous living spaces designed for hosting. The grounds extend the resort-like feel, with landscaped areas, a swimming pool and a fountain surrounding the main residence. There is also a separate one-bedroom guesthouse and staff quarters, giving the estate additional privacy and flexibility for visitors.From Hollywood to Harry And MeghanThe New York Post report also states that the property has had an unusually starry guest list. Over the years, it has reportedly hosted Oprah Winfrey and former President Barack Obama. Its most closely watched chapter came in 2020, when Prince Harry and Meghan Markle stayed at the estate after relocating to the United States. Perry provided the couple with both a home and security as they established themselves in California. The Duke and Duchess of Sussex eventually left California and returned to the United Kingdom after several years in the US, but their stay cemented the Beverly Hills property’s place in the celebrity real estate conversation.Another trophy property for saleThe Beverly Hills listing is not Perry’s only major property to hit the market this year. The report also states that in June, he listed his Jackson Hole, Wyoming, retreat for $39.5 million. The property spans 37.62 acres and includes an approximately 10,988-square-foot custom log home. With both properties listed, Perry is seeking a combined $96.5 million. The sales come as the filmmaker prepares for a significant change in his lifestyle and work routine.Preparing for Puerto RicoAccording to the New York Post, Perry, 57, has said he plans to relocate to Puerto Rico at the beginning of 2027 while reducing the pace of his professional schedule. The move represents a notable shift for a filmmaker whose career has been closely tied to Atlanta and Los Angeles. His property portfolio remains extensive, including a large residence near Atlanta and Tyler Perry Studios, his 330-acre production complex built on the site of a former Army base. He has also owned property in the Bahamas’ Exuma Cays.A resilient Beverly Hills marketPerry’s asking price arrives against a complicated backdrop for Los Angeles luxury real estate. High-end properties have faced pressure from the city’s mansion tax and the wider impact of recent wildfires. Beverly Hills, however, has continued to command substantial prices. The median sale price reached $4 million during the three months ending in August, representing a 34.1% increase from the same period a year earlier, according to Redfin. Against that backdrop, Perry’s estate enters the market not merely as another celebrity home, but as a substantial piece of Beverly Hills real estate with a history of its own.Images Courtesy: Wikipedia and New York PostReady to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Is Spain’s anti-eviction decree a fix for its housing crisis?
articles.summary: The government blames ‘savage speculation’ as critics say new measures leave small landlords ‘out in the cold’.
articles.body:
Spain’s left-wing coalition government has announced measures to ban evictions until 2030 to address the country’s housing crisis, after the forced removal of an 87-year-old woman last week triggered mass protests.

The new measures, ⁠including rolling over contracts and banning so-called vulture funds from the housing market, will be divided into two decrees to be voted on Friday in parliament, where Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s minority left government will face an uphill battle to secure support.

Spain’s housing crisis has driven a sharp political and social split between renters and property owners, with critics saying the proposed measures risk unfairly lumping small landlords who rely on rental income together with profit-driven real estate companies.

Health Minister Monica Garcia has framed parliament’s approval as non-negotiable, after a similar decree seeking to roll over rental contracts was blocked in April by right-leaning parties.

“Right-wing parties have to choose: either they’re with the citizens, or they’re with the foreign vulture funds,” she said on X on Wednesday. “Let them prove their patriotism beyond bracelets and flags.”

“And if they don’t, may it cost them dearly,” she added.

Why did the eviction of an elderly woman cause outrage?

The eviction of wheelchair user Maricarmen Abascal, who was removed from her home of more than seven decades on a stretcher last week, drew more than 10,000 protesters to the streets.

Abascal was living in the property in Madrid’s central Retiro neighbourhood under a rent-capped lease contract signed by her father in the 1950s. The property was then bought by the real estate and investment firm Urbagestion in 2018.

Urbagestion sought to terminate Abascal’s contract and evict her after raising her rent from 500 euros ($572) to 2,650 euros ($3,010) – nearly double her pension of €1,350 ($1,533) a month – according to Spanish newspaper El Pais.

When the police carried out her eviction on their fourth attempt on September 23, hundreds of activists who had been protesting against her losing a home she had lived in her entire life were waiting outside.

The videos of Abascal’s personal struggle made the rounds on social media, turning the 87-year-old into a symbol of Spain’s housing crisis.

Spontaneous demonstrations began the same day in front of a controversial luxury penthouse that the Madrid regional government, led by Isabel Diaz Ayuso of the conservative People’s Party (PP), recently purchased for unclear purposes.

Protesters cried out: “Ayuso’s penthouse for Maricarmen!” and “Shame! Shame!”

The platform #Niundesahuciomas (Not One More Eviction) called for simultaneous protests in Avila, Barcelona, Cadiz, Oviedo, Sevilla and Valencia.

Speaking at the recently concluded United Nations General Assembly, Sanchez, of the Socialist Party, described evictions as “a social tragedy that we cannot accept as a country” and blamed the local and regional governments of Madrid led by the People’s Party (PP).

Housing Minister Isabel Rodriguez Garcia said that the eviction “evidences the consequences of savage speculation and of rolling out the red carpet to the vultures and the speculators”.

According to data collected by the Bank of Spain reported by El Pais, real estate wealth now exceeds €7.4 trillion ($9.53 trillion), but the gains are far from evenly distributed. Property wealth is highly concentrated, with the richest 10 percent of households owning about one-third of all real estate wealth, while the bottom half owns only about 15 percent.

Additionally, the number of owners with two, five or more properties was found to have risen significantly, while the share of small owners with just one property declined.

The minister said the government was seeking to broaden the definition of what constitutes a vulture fund beyond large private equity funds to any fund or company that buys housing for speculation.

The minister named investment firm Urbagestion, which owns Abascal’s apartment, as an example of a firm that might fall into that category.

Abascal’s lawyer Beatriz Duro said on Tuesday that Urbagestion had offered a preliminary agreement that would allow her return to her home, paying 30 percent ⁠of her pension over the next eight years, equivalent to about 500 euros a month.

Why is there controversy over the proposed reforms?

Junts, the Catalan pro-independence party that would need to back the decree for it to pass, said on Tuesday it was still far from agreeing on all measures and wanted safeguards for small landlords, who make up the vast majority of property owners in Spain and who would be treated the same as large institutional investors.

The party’s parliamentary spokesperson Miriam Nogueras said the agreement left “small landlords out in the cold”.

“We all agreed that evictions – where the property is owned by a fund, a vulture fund, run by someone managing millions of euros – obviously need ⁠to be stopped,” she said on RTVE.

“Lumping together in this category those who have invested their savings in a flat, a restaurant or a property – putting them all in the same basket – is a mistake.”

Alberto Nunez Feijoo, the leader of the conservative PP, said “eight years adrift in housing policy aren’t fixed with an 11th-hour decree” and that his party would not support the legislation in parliament.

Feijoo had previously argued that tackling the housing crisis required dramatically increasing supply and offering major tax incentives for young buyers, opting for market expansion rather than government regulation.

Over the past decade, home prices have increased by almost 50 percent while not enough properties are available for rent. Spain’s National Statistics Institute (INE) found the national housing price index more than doubled since 2014, with prices 2.3 times higher than in Madrid.

INE data also showed that the cost of housing was absorbing a large share of household income. In 2024, 28.1 percent of people renting a home at market rates were spending more than 40 percent of their disposable income on housing, compared with an average in the European Union of 19.2 percent.

Marta Soler Gallart, head of the Department of Sociology at the University of Barcelona, said that neither of the two decrees addresses the problem in the medium and long term.

“Models such as Vienna’s, with its low rents, are cited in support of these decrees, but it is overlooked that the Vienna model and others have low rents because of their long history of creating and maintaining public social housing,” Soler Gallart told Al Jazeera. “In Spain, however, public funds are invested in social housing which, after a while, the recipients sell at market price.”

Soler Gallart also said the new measures disadvantage small landlords by extending five-year tenancy agreements by a further two years and by providing an indefinite extension of their tenancy agreements.

“However, these extensions are not compulsory if the landlord can prove that they need the property for their own use,” she said.

articles.title: Ole Miss students' toxicology reports will be done 'in due course,' families to be notified first: officials
articles.summary: Ole Miss students Aidan Hamilton and Robert Strang were found dead with Smax synthetic kratom tablets near them, officials said.
articles.body: The toxicology reports for two Ole Miss students who died on Sept. 21 will be completed "in due course," with the families being notified of results first, an official tells Fox News Digital. Ole Miss students Aidan Hamilton, 18, and Robert Strang, 20, were found dead on Sept. 21, both with similar packages of kratom or synthetic kratom found to be in their possession, according to the court documents. Officials detailed that Hamilton "could have died due to a Pulmonary Edema," which would be consistent with a drug overdose. Strang was found "cold to the touch" when first responders arrived at his house near campus. Alex Gibert, press secretary for the Mississippi Department of Public Safety, told Fox News Digital: "Commissioner met with the [medical examiner's] Office yesterday and we expect the reports to be finalized ‘in due course.’ The families will be the first to know." The news comes as the American Kratom Association hosted a news conference on Wednesday, criticizing the "delay in publicly identifying the specific products purchased by two Ole Miss students before their deaths." The group says these tablets "are not natural kratom leaf and that students should have been specifically warned about these products under investigation." VAPE STORE CLERK NEAR OLE MISS CAMPUS WARNED BUYER 'PEOPLE WERE DYING' FROM KRATOM PILLS, AFFIDAVIT SAYS Packaging on the kratom items found near both men were labeled "Smax, Pseudo-DHM" tablets, which is a "Kratom like substance at gas stations or tobacco shops" that people buy for the "narcotic like effect," according to the court documents. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB Hamilton made several purchases in September at Puffs Vape, Tobacco and Beer Store in Oxford, where workers Yahya Mohamed Mosleh, 51, and Islam Mohamed, 18, were arrested and face a charge of possession of a controlled substance with intent to distribute. Officials did not say in the court documents that the kratom found near him when he died came from that store. One of the purchases was made one day before Hamilton was found dead. LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST One hour after finding Hamilton dead, police were dispatched to a house near campus and found Strang dead. A package of the "Smax, Pseudo-DHM" tablets was found on his nightstand, along with 20 to 30 nitrous oxide cans, known as "whippets," which Strang's roommates said he used daily. Strang's roommates told officers that he was watching football and took a Xanax bar the day before being found dead. GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL Officials said the synthetic kratom-derived product Strang had bought was purchased at a gas station about 30 minutes away from Oxford. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The precise role kratom played in the deaths of Hamilton and Strang has not yet been determined. articles.title: Operation Sheruwali: How security forces tracked LeT commander Musa in months-long hunt since May
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The killing of senior Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) commander Mohammad Asif alias Hashim Musa in Jammu and Kashmir's Budgam district on Wednesday was
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The killing of senior Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) commander Mohammad Asif alias Hashim Musa in Jammu and Kashmir's Budgam district on Wednesday was the culmination of a months-long intelligence-led operation, named ‘Operation Sheruwali’, launched in May 2026.Security forces had been tracking Musa for a prolonged period before a coordinated plan involving multiple agencies was drawn up to neutralise him, following the receipt of technical and human intelligence about his movements and presence in the area.The operation culminated in an encounter in the Yousmarg area of Budgam, where Musa was killed. His body was later recovered along with war-like stores, according to the Army.Also read| Ex-Pakistan SSG commando, highly trained LeT terrorist, Pahalgam mastermind: Who was Hashim Moosa; killed in J&K encounterThe ministry of information and broadcasting said the operation dealt a blow to the LeT network in Jammu and Kashmir, with Musa's killing bringing an end to a group of four senior commanders who had been operating in the union territory since 2022 and were linked to several attacks.How Operation Sheruwali unfoldedAccording to a statement issued by the Press Information Bureau (PIB), security forces had been pursuing Musa for a long time. A specific plan involving all stakeholders was recently put in place after intelligence inputs indicated his movement and presence.The government said the operation to neutralise Musa was part of the ongoing ‘Operation Sheruwali’, which began in May 2026.The Army's Chinar Corps, meanwhile, said the encounter took place during Operation Korag in the Yousmarg area of Budgam district. Troops launched a search operation based on specific intelligence inputs and challenged suspicious movement, following which terrorists opened fire.The operation involved the Indian Army, Jammu and Kashmir Police and the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF).The search continued after the encounter, with security personnel checking the surrounding areas for any additional terrorist presence. Musa's body was recovered from the general area of Palmaidan along with war-like stores, according to the Chinar Corps.Is Hashim Moosa an ex-Pakistan SSG commando?One of the key aspects of Musa's background is his alleged association with Pakistan's military.ANI, quoting security agency sources, reported that Musa had served as a para-commando in Pakistan's Special Service Group (SSG), where he held the rank of Havildar. According to the sources, he retired from the SSG in 2023, subsequently joined the LeT and infiltrated into India.Former Jammu and Kashmir DGP S P Vaid described Musa as a highly trained commando specialising in ambushes and guerrilla-style attacks.Vaid alleged that Musa's footprints had been seen in several attacks in Jammu and Kashmir, including those in Poonch, DKG, Bhimber Gali, Gulmarg and the attack on pilgrims in Reasi.However, his alleged military background has been reported by security agency sources and has not been independently established.Four-member LeT group neutralisedWith Musa's killing, all four senior LeT commanders belonging to the group that had been active in Jammu and Kashmir since 2022 have been neutralised, according to the government.The three other commanders were killed in separate encounters:Junaid Bhat: Neutralised on December 3, 2024, in Dachigam.Suleman: Killed on July 28, 2025, during Operation Mahadev.Yasir: Neutralised on September 4, 2026, during Operation Asdhar.The government linked the group to several attacks across Jammu and Kashmir, including the Halan attack in August 2023, DKG attack in December 2023, Kandi attack in May 2023, Shahsitar attack in May 2024, Shiv Khori attack in June 2024, Gagangir and Bootapathri attacks in October 2024, and the Baisaran attack in April 2025.Musa's alleged role in Pahalgam attackMusa was among the key suspects in the April 22, 2025, Pahalgam terror attack, in which terrorists targeted tourists at Baisaran Valley, killing 26 people.The Jammu and Kashmir Police had announced a reward of Rs 20 lakh for information leading to the arrest of Pakistan nationals and LeT terrorists Adil Hussain Thoker, Ali Bhai and Hashim Musa.The National Investigation Agency (NIA) subsequently chargesheeted seven accused in the case, including Pakistan-based LeT and The Resistance Front (TRF), which it accused of planning, facilitating and executing the attack.The NIA's 1,597-page chargesheet also named Pakistani handler Sajid Jatt as an accused and detailed the alleged Pakistan-based conspiracy behind the attack.The government said the operation reflected sustained coordination between the Jammu and Kashmir Police, the Indian Army and Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs) in counter-terrorism operations across the union territory.Get the latest India News and Live articles.title: Florida judge rips into mom accused of leaving 4 children at home to go on 3-day cruise
articles.summary: Bodycam footage showed four children hiding in a bathroom after Nathalie Belizaire allegedly left them alone to board the Carnival Conquest.
articles.body: A Florida mother is facing four felony charges after allegedly abandoning her four young children — including a 2-month-old infant — to take a three-day vacation on a cruise ship to the Bahamas. Nathalie Belizaire, 29, was charged with four counts of child neglect after she boarded Carnival Cruise Line’s Carnival Conquest, leaving her children unattended in her North Miami Beach residence. Police said U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers took her into custody Monday as she disembarked. "You cannot make this up," Miami-Dade Circuit Judge Mindy Glazer said in Tuesday court footage. "We are just grateful nothing worse happened to those kids. MOTHER, BOYFRIEND ALLEGEDLY ABANDONED BLINDFOLDED YOUNG SONS IN REMOTE FOREST AS PART OF 'GAME': REPORTS "Who leaves four little kids alone to go on a cruise? "The poor kids were home alone." The children were discovered by police Saturday, the day after the ship set sail. Bodycam footage showed four kids coming out of hiding in a bathroom – a 2-year-old toddler, a pre-teen and what appeared to be a teenage girl holding a newborn baby. Lether Bazile, the father of the 2-month-old, told police that Belizaire claimed she was leaving the children with their great-grandmother, the New York Post reported. BABYSITTER ACCUSED OF KIDNAPPING TWO YOUNG SISTERS WAS PREVIOUSLY CHARGED WITH ABDUCTING NEWBORN The father was tipped off by the mother's absence by Belizaire’s WhatsApp story two days earlier that appeared to show a Carnival Cruise Line ticket, he told police. When Bazile stopped by Belizaire's home, he saw the television glowing through the blinds and heard the children's voices inside. He immediately called the police, who entered the home and found the four children hiding in a bathroom with no adult present. According to authorities, the children's grandmother, Denise Wilkes, told officers that Belizaire had promised to drop the kids off but never showed up. Furthermore, Belizaire’s brother, Steven Borgella, informed police that his sister had texted him at 8 p.m. ET on the day the children were found, asking him to check in on them. ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHARGED WITH ABUSING HER KIDS, SETTING FIRE IN HOUSE WHILE MAKING MENTAL HEALTH DEFENSE Belizaire was arrested Monday as she disembarked the vessel at the port in Miami. She declined to speak to officers. During the Tuesday hearing, Belizaire’s defense attorney argued that her abandoning the children to go on vacation was "just an allegation at this time," noting that she denies the claims. "At this time, it is only an allegation; she denies the allegation," the defense attorney said. "Of course she does," Glazer said as the accused showed exasperation. "They arrested her disembarking from the cruise ship!" the judge then shot back. TWO MISSING CHILDREN RESCUED FROM TRAILER AS POLICE ARREST BABYSITTER ON KIDNAPPING CHARGES "I understand that, judge, I understand that," the attorney replied. "The question is who was the one responsible for the children at the time?" Glazer thought for a second, before saying, "usually it's the mother, the person that gave birth to them." "There are also others responsible, it's not just mothers," the defense attorney replied. "It's not just mothers that are in charge of children, judge. It's also fathers and grandparents and other people." "See, the mothers always know who their children are," Glazer said. "Fathers may not know, but it looks like different fathers here. One of the fathers grew concerned and called the police." Belizaire was given a stay away order until the Department of Children and Families can investigate. She faces four felony counts of child neglect without great bodily harm. Bond was set at $10,000, $2,500 per child. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP This recent arrest is not Belizaire's first run-in with the law. She previously faced aggravated battery charges in January 2025 after allegedly pepper-spraying a neighbor in the face during a dispute regarding her daughter, the Post reported.

articles.title: What happened on diverted Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv?
articles.summary: Israel’s prime minister said one of the pilots stabbed the other and then tried to crash the plane.
articles.body:
A flight from the United Arab Emirates to Israel was diverted to Saudi Arabia after issuing a distress signal in what appeared to be a hijacking attempt on Wednesday.

The Flydubai flight FZ1073 was diverted as it flew from Dubai to Tel Aviv through Jordanian airspace, prompting Israel to deploy warplanes, the Reuters news agency reported.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said one of the pilots had stabbed the other and then tried to crash the plane. He added that Israel was preparing for other “potential threats” after the incident.

Flydubai said an altercation had occurred on the flight deck and that all passengers were safe and accounted for. The plane was secured by on-duty crew travelling onboard, it added.

“At this early stage, the underlying reasons and motives behind this event are unknown and remain subject to a formal investigation,” a Flydubai spokesperson said in a statement. “We urge all parties to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts.”

At Saudi Arabia’s Tabuk airport, where the plane landed, officials said both the plane’s captain and first officer were taken to hospital after sustaining injuries, according to a statement from the Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz International Airport in Tabuk, carried by the Saudi state-run Al Ekhbariya television.

India’s embassy in Saudi Arabia later identified the injured captain as Indian national Smit Machchhar. The embassy said he was receiving treatment at a hospital in Tabuk and was reported to be in stable condition, adding that it was in contact with his family and Saudi authorities.

The UAE has become a popular holiday destination for Israeli tourists since the countries normalised ties in 2020 . Here’s what we know about what happened.

Footage taken onboard the plane appears to show the injured pilot lying on the cabin floor with several stab wounds, and a passenger with a bloody wound to the head.

In another video, passengers weep and cry out in distress as the aircraft shakes.

Yasmin Abukasis, the mother of one of the passengers onboard, said her daughter Miriam thought she was going to die. “The plane started to lose control,” she told journalists at Israel’s Ben Gurion airport, before other pilots onboard took control of the aircraft.

Flight tracking data indicated the plane descended about 14,000 feet (4,300 metres) in less than 30 seconds about two and a half hours after leaving Dubai. Flightradar24 said on X that an initial general emergency signal designated by code 7700 was issued at about 05:31 GMT and was later changed to another emergency signal with code 7500 declaring “unlawful interference”.

Passenger Dalia Shpigel told Israeli newspaper Haaretz that some people seated towards the front of the plane broke into the cockpit after the plane began to descend and they realised something was wrong.

“An hour before landing, we felt that there was no control over the plane, that it was starting to jump,” she said. “The guys saw that the plane had begun to dive and broke into the cockpit.”

Netanyahu said he later spoke to one of the Israeli passengers who broke into the cockpit and overpowered one of the pilots who was reportedly trying to sabotage the aircraft’s systems.

“I salute these heroes who demonstrated extraordinary resourcefulness and courage,” Netanyahu said in a statement. “They saved many lives and prevented a major disaster.”

Passenger Yitzhak Lieber, reportedly one of the men who overpowered the co-pilot, sent a video to his family from the plane, international media reported. In it, he says: “There is a pilot who was seriously injured, they’ve evacuated him. We overpowered the terrorist and he is tied up.”

articles.title: A Texas family has owned land in Freeport since 1940; after the port sought to seize it in 2020, a private fruit warehouse rose on the property, and the family is fighting another court defeat in 2026
articles.summary: A Texas family that has owned land in Freeport since 1940 is preparing to file a new legal appeal after a state trial court ruled against them in an
articles.body: A Texas family that has owned land in Freeport since 1940 is preparing to file a new legal appeal after a state trial court ruled against them in an ongoing fight over eminent domain. A Texas trial court granted summary judgment against the Marshall family and other landowners in Freeport's historically Black East End neighborhood. The ruling allows Port Freeport to continue taking private property, where a cold-storage fruit warehouse for a private company has already been built next to their land. With support from the public-interest law firm Institute for Justice, the Marshall family plans to challenge the ruling before the Texas Court of Appeals. The legal team argues that the port authority is using public taking powers to support private commercial projects instead of a valid public purpose. "The Texas Constitution is clear on this matter and we plan on making that clear before the Texas Court of Appeals," said Institute for Justice Senior Attorney Jeffrey Redfern in a statement released by the organization. "The government cannot just use eminent domain to take the Marshalls' land simply because the Port thought it could. The Constitution demands more."Decades of family ownership in the East EndThe dispute goes back to 1940, when the Marshall family first bought land in the East End section of Freeport. The neighborhood was established in the 1920s and was the only part of the coastal town where Black residents were legally allowed to live. Over the years, generations of the Marshall family built homes, ran small businesses, and raised children on these properties. But as shipping and maritime trade grew along the Gulf Coast, Port Freeport began buying land across the East End for industrial development. By 2020, Port Freeport had started formal eminent domain proceedings to take the Marshall family's remaining land. The port authority said the property was needed for maritime infrastructure projects. While property owners went to court to protect their deeds, construction continued nearby. Port authorities approved a temperature-controlled fruit warehouse built specifically to serve a private agricultural importer.Warehouse expansion sparks constitutional fightLawyers for the Marshall family say using public condemnation powers to support commercial buildings crosses a constitutional line. Under state and federal law, government entities may use eminent domain only when land is intended for direct public use, such as roads, public utilities, or civic infrastructure. During the early stages of the case, court filings showed that Port Freeport planned to give seized land parcels to private corporate tenants. Public-interest lawyers argue that taking property from private owners and giving it to other private companies violates Article I, Section 17 of the Texas Constitution. Property rights advocates say this follows a pattern seen in earlier eminent domain disputes. In those cases, public agencies used economic development arguments to replace established residential neighborhoods with commercial facilities. Earlier in the case, the Texas 14th Court of Appeals issued a ruling in favor of East End landowners. It rejected an earlier effort by Port Freeport to take parcels without clear public development plans. However, the latest trial court summary judgment put the land titles at risk again, leading to an immediate notice of appeal.Broader legal precedent for private propertyThe appeal could have wider effects on property rights across Texas. Public-interest legal advocates say that if port authorities can take decades-old residential and family-owned lots for commercial storage facilities, small landowners near city industrial areas could have little protection. The Institute for Justice has handled similar property rights cases across the United States. These include ongoing disputes in Georgia and New York, where local authorities sought to take private parcels for commercial reuse. For the Marshall family, the case is a fight to protect eight decades of family history in a neighborhood built by their ancestors during a time of enforced segregation. The case will now move to the Texas Court of Appeals. articles.title: Romania’s political crisis intensifies as Parliament rejects pro-EU PM
articles.summary: Siegfried Muresan’s loss of the confidence motion increases the prospect for snap elections.
articles.body:
Romania’s pro-European Prime Minister-designate Siegfried Muresan has failed to win a parliamentary vote of confidence, prolonging a political crisis seen as a boost for the rising far right.

Muresan, a liberal European Parliament member who was the latest of three designated prime ministers, secured only 182 votes out of the 233 required to secure the confidence motion on Wednesday, according to the official count.

The far-right Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR) largely boycotted the vote.

The 45-year-old had proposed what he described as a “reform-oriented” governing programme under his centre-right National Liberal Party (PNL), which teamed up with the Save Romania Union party, or USR, and the small ethnic Hungarian UDMR party.

President Nicusor Dan said he would nominate a new prime minister candidate on Monday afternoon, after holding talks with the leaders of the parliamentary parties, to avoid snap elections.

Romania saw the collapse of a pro-European coalition government in May, when governing social democrats, together with the opposition far right, ousted liberal Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan in a no-confidence motion at that time.

The far right, which comprises about a third of Parliament, threatened to impeach the president if he does not call early elections once the conditions are met.

Romania, a member of the EU and NATO that borders Ukraine, has not held snap elections since the fall of communism in 1989.

Political analyst Cristian Pirvulescu told the AFP news agency that snap elections would lead to another fragmented Parliament, but with an emboldened far right.

“Early elections mean that, from the moment they are called, it would take four months before a new government could be formed,” Pirvulescu told AFP. “Due to political instability, Romania finds itself in a very complicated economic situation. Four months is already a very long time.”

The country of 19 million has been struggling for months with the highest public deficit and inflation in the European Union.
