articles.title: US appeals court halts Tennessee execution of Christa Pike
articles.summary: Christa Pike was set to become the first woman executed by Tennessee in more than 200 years.
articles.body:
A federal appeals court has temporarily stopped Tennessee from executing death row inmate Christa Pike , intervening less than two hours before she was due to receive a lethal injection.

The 6th US Circuit Court of Appeals granted what it called a “short stay of execution” on Wednesday while judges consider Pike’s argument that evidence of sexual abuse she experienced as a child was not properly weighed when she was sentenced.

Tennessee officials quickly turned to the US Supreme Court, asking the justices to lift the stay and allow the execution to proceed.

Pike, 50, had been scheduled to die at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville. Had the execution gone ahead, she would have been the first woman executed by Tennessee in more than two centuries.

She was sentenced to death for the 1995 killing of Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old classmate at a Knoxville vocational centre.

Pike was 18 when she, her 17-year-old boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp, and another teenager tortured and killed Slemmer. Pike and Shipp were later convicted of first-degree murder. Shipp received a life sentence with the possibility of parole.

Pike’s lawyers have argued that her childhood was marked by violence, neglect and sexual abuse, including rapes when she was 11 and 17 years old. They also cited her later diagnoses of bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder in seeking to have her sentence reduced to life without parole.

Tennessee Governor Bill Lee rejected that clemency request. Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, has publicly supported the execution.

The case has also attracted international scrutiny, with a group of United Nations human rights experts calling for Pike’s death sentence to be commuted.

Women have accounted for just 18 of the 1,683 executions carried out in the US since capital punishment resumed in 1976. Pike’s case is more unusual still: If the execution ultimately proceeds, she would be the only person in Tennessee’s modern death penalty era put to death for a crime committed as a teenager.

articles.title: MI5 warns UK academics to cut ties with Chinese group over alleged spying
articles.summary: UK intelligence agency accuses Chinese institute of funding academic research to boost Beijing’s espionage capability.
articles.body:
Britain’s domestic intelligence agency has told academics to stop working with a Chinese organisation funding research in United Kingdom universities, accusing it of having “very strong ties” with China’s spy agency.

In a rare public espionage alert on Wednesday, MI5 alleged the ⁠⁠”primary purpose” of the China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI) is to finance academic work that improves the espionage capability of the Ministry of State Security (MSS), the Chinese intelligence agency.

There was no immediate response from Beijing, which has previously strongly denied such accusations.

MI5 said the CGTRI targeted more than 100 UK-based academics working in areas such as artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, covert communications systems and steganography.

It said many academics and institutions would have engaged in good faith with the organisation, unaware of its close ties to the MSS. But it added those who continued to take grants from or work with the CGTRI now risked prosecution under the UK’s National Security Act, a law passed in 2023 that gave the government greater powers to target foreign espionage and hostile state activities.

“This activity supports MSS espionage, which poses a threat to UK national security,” MI5 said.

UK Security Minister ⁠⁠Dan Jarvis said he had written to all university leaders in Britain to ensure staff ended any relationship with the CGTRI.

“This alert exposes attempts by Chinese intelligence to covertly benefit from the expertise and research of our academics, undermining our national security, and that of our allies,” he said in a statement.

“International ⁠⁠partnerships are vital to ensure our universities and research institutes continue to thrive, but we will take robust action to defend against the threats we face.”

The UK’s relationship with China, its third largest trading partner, has become ⁠⁠increasingly complex in recent years.

The government in London has sought ⁠⁠better relations with Beijing to improve trade ties and earlier this year approved plans for China to build its largest embassy in Europe in the UK capital. But it has also repeatedly warned of Chinese spying efforts and attempts to undermine the UK’s democratic system.

Last year, Ken McCallum, MI5’s director-general, said Chinese spies were creating fake job adverts to try to dupe British professionals into handing over data.

His agency also issued an alert to UK lawmakers last November that Chinese agents were targeting them to collect information and influence their activity by posing as headhunters or companies.

In ‌‌June, ‌‌security agencies from the Five Eyes intelligence alliance – the US, Britain, Canada, Australia and New Zealand – published a warning about Chinese spies aggressively using online job platforms to recruit people with access to sensitive information.

China’s London embassy said the warning was “entirely fabricated and constitutes malicious slander”.

articles.title: Irish PM says Ireland ‘not overrun’ by immigrants, legal migration tied to economic success
articles.summary: Micheál Martin addresses Ireland's demographic change as nearly one in four in Ireland are born abroad as the government moves to tighten asylum, citizenship and immigration rules.
articles.body: NEW YORK — Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin pushed back on the notion that Ireland has been "overrun" by immigrants as nearly one in four residents is now foreign-born, arguing that the country's dramatic demographic change has been driven largely by legal migration tied to its economic success story. Martin, in an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital, acknowledged failures in Ireland's asylum system after a record surge in applications, saying it "was too slow" in recent years. He also addressed moves to tighten citizenship rules and opened the door to publishing crime statistics by nationality amid a heated debate over immigration and crime. The issue has become a political flashpoint across Europe and the U.S. and comes weeks after President Donald Trump warned about Europe's approach while appearing alongside Martin in Dublin. "That immigration, what you're doing to yourselves, you're just killing yourselves," Trump said. TRUMP SAYS HE WOULD 'LOVE' TO SEE IRELAND UNIFIED AS ONE NATION "Ireland is not overrun in any shape or form," Martin told Fox News Digital. "But we are conscious that it is an issue that has to be addressed robustly, firmly, fairly as well in terms of those seeking asylum." "All over Europe it's tightening up because of the pressures and migration has created significant political pressures across Europe," he added. "Obviously, illegal migration is the more potent issue. And our system was too slow in processing those seeking asylum. That has changed. We've accelerated the application and the consideration of applications, and we've also now accelerated the appeals process." Martin said his government is developing a new migration strategy that includes proposals to increase residency requirements for citizenship from five to eight years and introduce language and economic self-sufficiency requirements. Migration and crime Immigration has become increasingly intertwined in Ireland's political debate with concerns over housing, crime and rapidly changing demographics in a country that was drastically more homogeneous a generation ago. The issue burst into international view in November 2023, after Algerian-born Irish citizen Riad Bouchaker stabbed three young children and a childcare worker outside a school in Dublin, triggering riots as anger among some opponents of mass immigration spilled into violence on the streets of the capital. The unrest was followed by sustained opposition to government efforts to house asylum seekers in communities across the country, with some protests also descending into violent clashes. Immigration returned to the spotlight this summer following the violent killing of Jamey Carney, a 43-year-old American mother from New York who was found dead at her home in County Kerry. Her Jordanian boyfriend, the suspect in the case, had applied for asylum in Ireland but was rejected and was appealing the decision while remaining in the country. He fled Ireland for Turkey shortly after the killing, later traveling to Jordan and Irish police are now seeking his extradition. Fox News Digital asked Martin whether the case exposed weaknesses in Ireland's immigration system and whether laws needed to be changed. "We're looking at all of that in terms of tightening up the laws," Martin said. "We will make sure that, particularly if people's applications are rejected, that there's fast movement in terms of the consequences of that." MIGRANT WHO FLED IRELAND AFTER AMERICAN MOTHER'S MURDER IS ARRESTED IN JORDAN Crime data Critics of Ireland's immigration policies have argued that migrants are disproportionately responsible for crime, while opponents of that view say such claims unfairly stigmatize the country's growing foreign-born population. But the debate has been difficult to settle because Irish national crime statistics do not routinely publish nationality breakdowns, leaving limited public data to test competing claims. The lack of data has prompted calls for greater transparency from women's advocates and some Irish lawmakers, including proposals to publish crime statistics broken down by nationality. "I've no issue with data ... because that can inform, because sometimes you get a kind of distorted picture," Martin said when asked whether crime statistics should include the nationality of alleged suspects. "So as far as I'm concerned, data is important." But Martin pushed back on the argument that nationality itself drives crime. "I don't think crime is specific to any nationality," he said. "But there are issues there, and in some cases, yes, there's been horrific crimes committed, but not all by illegal migrants either." Housing pressures Housing has become another flashpoint as Ireland struggles to build enough homes to keep pace with its growing population. Martin acknowledged that workers arriving legally in Ireland add to housing demand but said his government’s answer is to increase supply, with about 36,000 homes built last year, up more than 20% from the previous year and the highest annual total since 2011. The Irish government's reliance on hotels and other properties to house asylum seekers has itself become a flashpoint. The state spent about $1.4 billion on asylum accommodation and related services in 2025, while also buying properties outright, including the sprawling Citywest Hotel and Convention Centre for about $175 million. The allocation of scarce public housing has further fueled the immigration debate. The pressure is particularly acute in Dublin, where figures released by the city council this month showed 42% of the 15,005 households on its social-housing waiting list were categorized as non-Irish, fueling anger online as Ireland's homeless population hit a record high last month. Nationally, 28.7% of social housing applicants — nearly 18,000 households — were non-Irish citizens in 2025, according to government figures provided to Fox News Digital. That included nearly 3,200 applicants from outside the EU with refugee status, up 64% from the previous year. Asked whether Irish citizens should receive preferential treatment for social housing amid pressure on waiting lists, Martin backed the idea, saying that "our position is basically its citizens get priority." WATCH: Irish PM Micheál Martin addresses immigration's impact on Ireland's housing crisis A country transformed Ireland's demographic transformation has been rapid. Nearly one in four people living in Ireland was born abroad, up from about one in seven two decades ago. At 23.3%, Ireland now has the fourth-highest percentage of foreign-born residents in the European Union, according to Eurostat. The transformation accelerated after the EU expanded eastward in 2004, a decision that helped fuel a sharp rise in immigration during Ireland's "Celtic Tiger" economic boom, when years of rapid growth transformed the country from one of Western Europe's poorer economies into one of its wealthiest. "It's a bit like America really, free movement for the states here," Martin said. "Our economy's expanded hugely." Martin pointed to financial services and medical devices as industries that rely on skilled foreign workers, including non-EU workers arriving on work permits. More than half a million non-EU citizens were living in Ireland at the start of 2025, accounting for 9.3% of the population, according to Eurostat. "It has been very dramatic, I agree, in the last three decades, largely because of the economic growth of Ireland," Martin said. "You can't switch off an economy either." WATCH: Irish PM says legal immigration fueled Ireland's economic success story Ireland's economy has undergone a remarkable turnaround since the economic stagnation of the 1980s, through the "Celtic Tiger" boom and a devastating crash in 2008, before rebounding strongly. Over those decades, Ireland became a major European base for U.S. multinationals including Apple, Meta, Pfizer and Johnson & Johnson. Martin has been at the center of Irish politics through much of that period, serving in successive Fianna Fáil-led governments from 1997 before becoming prime minister, or Taoiseach, in 2020 and returning to the post in 2025. Ireland's economy continued to expand in 2025, with GDP growing 8%, according to Ireland's Central Statistics Office (CSO). But prosperity has not eliminated pressure on households: nearly 45% reported difficulty making ends meet, while 64% identified housing and the same share identified inflation and the cost of living as among Ireland's most pressing problems, according to the CSO. Ireland's more recent migration pressures have included a post-pandemic surge in asylum applicants, including people arriving from Africa, the Middle East and elsewhere. Applications jumped from roughly 3,500 a year before COVID to a record 18,561 in 2024, before falling nearly 30% last year and continuing to decline in 2026. Separately, more than 120,000 Ukrainians fleeing Russia's invasion arrived under the EU's Temporary Protection system rather than the asylum system. Martin said roughly 80,000 remain in Ireland, with many now working and contributing to the economy. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP A nation of emigrants Martin also emphasized that EU free movement works in both directions, with Irish citizens themselves living and working throughout the bloc. "Irish people are working and living all over Europe," Martin said. "That's the other side of that story and that is something perhaps that we're not as conscious of, but it is reality." Martin also placed Ireland's modern demographic transformation within the country's much longer history of emigration, pointing to the exodus that followed the Irish Famine. "Ireland had 8 million people in 1845 before the Great Famine. That led to the big wave of Irish people migrating to come to America," Martin said. "We're not at that level yet on the island of Ireland, so we need to look at it through the broad sweep of history in a historical perspective."

articles.title: U.S. ends ISIS-fighting mission in Iraq as regional security fears mount
articles.summary: The last American troops assigned to fight ISIS in Iraq pulled out of the country Wednesday, ending the mission that dismantled the extremists’ self-declared caliphate but raising fears about what might fill the vacuum as the Iran war grinds on.
articles.body: The last American troops assigned to fight ISIS in Iraq pulled out of the country Wednesday, ending the mission that dismantled the extremists’ self-declared caliphate but raising fears about what might fill the vacuum as the Iran war grinds on. Though the Iraqi government welcomed the end of Operation Inherent Resolve, Kurdish officials in the north of the country said they were concerned the Biden-era decision was being carried out even after Iranian missiles pummeled them following the war launched by the United States and Israel earlier this year. Iran-backed militias in Iraq have attacked U.S. personnel and diplomats, as well as regional allies such as Saudi Arabia. And there are fears Tehran could seek to capitalize on the U.S. withdrawal, with its proxies already celebrating the move, coupled with concerns about a potential resurgence in attacks by the remnants of the Islamic State terrorist group itself. “We came to fight a caliphate, and there is no longer a caliphate, so we are going home,” President Donald Trump said at the White House on Wednesday, adding that the moment was a “victory for the United States” as well as a “decisive victory over ISIS, which has been completely decimated, which is the reason we went in there in the first place.” Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said the “orderly departure” marked “the successful conclusion of the military mission that defeated ISIS in Iraq,” in a statement Wednesday. “This milestone reflects the success of a 12-year campaign that defeated ISIS as an organized military threat in Iraq and across the region.” The 2014 U.S.-led mission was successful in dismantling the “caliphate” ISIS governed across around 40% of Iraq and one third of Syria, sweeping through that territory amid instability that followed the U.S. invasion and subsequent withdrawal. But ISIS has not been defeated entirely in Iraq. The group comprises “hundreds of fighters” across seven provincial units, according to a United Nations monitoring report in August. This “limited presence” in desert areas generates $500,000 annually through extortion of farmers and shepherds, the report said. But it is “unable to conduct significant attacks” and is only capable of “unsophisticated operations” following the killing and arrest of leaders, it said. The U.S. expects Iraqi and Kurdish forces to now “lead the continuing effort to secure Iraq and keep ISIS remnants suppressed,” Parnell’s statement said. The Pentagon will “continue to provide targeted training and intelligence support to our Iraqi partners.” Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, who has been lavished with praise by Trump since entering office in July, described the withdrawal as the beginning of “a new phase.” At a handover ceremony in Baghdad, he said this would be “defined by Iraq’s sovereignty, the strength of its institutions, the readiness of its forces, the unity of its decision-making, and balanced partnerships with its friends.” However, Kurdish officials, who govern the north of Iraq, expressed alarm at the move. The Kurdish Peshmerga Affairs Ministry, which oversees defense, said Monday that the U.S. leaving without establishing any other air defense was “deeply concerning.” The withdrawal was agreed to under President Joe Biden’s administration in 2024, long before the Iran war drastically changed the region’s security landscape. The Peshmerga Ministry said Monday that 1,000 ballistic missiles have been fired at its territory by Iran since late February. “Some have hit civilian areas, inflicting injuries, material damage and deaths,” it said, nevertheless expressing “sincere gratitude” to the U.S. and its partners “for their cooperation and support.” The 2003 U.S.-led invasion saw around 150,000 American troops enter the country, toppling leader Saddam Hussein but also triggering a disastrous sectarian war. That combat operation came to an end in 2011, with almost all of the American personnel withdrawn. The U.S. returned to fight ISIS in 2014, with personnel numbers peaking at almost 9,000 as of 2017. That operation wound down in 2024, and until this week only a small contingent of around 1,500 remained in the Kurdish-governed north. After this week, a smaller contingent of U.S. forces will stay in Iraq to protect American diplomats. Iran-backed militant groups have already celebrated the milestone as “a ​historic victory,” as put by Abu Mojtaba al-Yasiri, a commander in the powerful umbrella group the Islamic Resistance in Iraq, who described it as “a crushing defeat for the American project.” And though depleted, ISIS itself “is seeking to send a message that the group is still powerful and capable of launching bloody attacks,” according to Col. Khalid al-Bayati, a senior security official in the strategic oil town of Kirkuk.

articles.title: Leeds Bradford Airport plan could see an extra 10 flights a night
articles.summary: LBA says there could be a 45% rise in night flights in summer if changes to current rules are approved.
articles.body:
Leeds Bradford Airport could run an extra 10 flights a night during the summer if changes to their operating rules are approved, the chief executive has said.

Currently the airport is permitted 2,920 aircraft movements between 23:00 and 07:00 BST annually, but bosses want to switch to a model that monitors overall noise levels instead of counting take-offs and landings.

It is also applying to condense night-time hours to between 23:30 and 05:59, with the plans set to be decided on by Leeds City Council later this autumn.

LBA say the changes would help the airport grow and keep airlines at the site, but campaigners say an increase in night flights would impact their ability to sleep.

During the summer time LBA operates about 18 night-time flights a day.

Asked by the BBC if the airport was simply trying to abolish the cap on night flights, chief executive Vincent Hodder said "absolutely not".

He said: "What we're doing is switching the focus from how many aircraft movements are taking place to what's actually really important here, which is how much noise is being produced by the aircraft operating out of the airport."

He said under the quota point system, an older, noisier plane would have more points than a newer, quieter plane, adding: "The way the limits in the application have been set - that 1,450 quota points - is to make sure that the level of noise we produce in future can never be any more than what is permitted to operate at the airport right now."

Hodder said the quota system the plan is based on was developed for London airports in the 1990s, and has been regularly updated since.

Hodder said more night flights would allow airlines to grow their business and create more jobs at the site.

"If we can't increase the level of flights at night then the airlines that currently base aircraft here, Jet2 and Ryanair - Jet2, one of our largest local employers – are unable to grow here at night because they don't have any night movements," he said.

"We're forced if we want to grow to move only towards quieter aircraft and that's how the incentive works."

As part of the proposals, the airport has offered a £5,500 grant to 700 residents who live on the flight path to spend on insulation or air conditioning so windows do not have to be kept shut on warm summer nights.

But, Cal Bailey who has lived under the flight path in Horsforth for 30 years said he was woken up frequently by night flights, and does not think insurance or air conditioning would help.

"I have insulated this house significantly since we moved in and air conditioning is not something I want to do. It's highly energy intensive," he said.

"I think local residents deserve to have the opportunity to sleep well at night."

articles.title: A political dynasty? Why the Bolsonaro family dominates Brazil’s right wing
articles.summary: For a third election in a row, a Bolsonaro family member is the leading right-wing contender for Brazil’s presidency.
articles.body:
Sao Paulo, Brazil – Much has changed since the far-right army captain Jair Bolsonaro won Brazil's presidency in 2018.

Last year, the former president was sentenced to 27 years in prison for attempting to overturn his 2022 election defeat. In 2023, he was barred from holding public office for eight years after a court determined he abused his political office.

He is currently banned from using social media. His last post was published in July 2025.

And yet, Bolsonaro has forged a powerful political dynasty that is on the verge of returning to power in Brazil's October presidential election.

His eldest son, 45-year-old Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, is in a statistical tie with the race's incumbent, left-leaning President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.

A September 24 poll released by the public opinion firm Datafolha showed Lula with a slim lead in a simulated run-off, earning 47 percent support to Flavio's 45 percent, well within the margin of error.

Other pollsters predict an even narrower gap between the two frontrunners.

Like his father, Flavio has faced investigation and scandal. But experts say the Bolsonaro family has endured as a political force in part by harnessing decades of frustration with Lula's Workers' Party (PT).

That resentment, in turn, has transformed into a potent election-season brand.

“There is a hyperfocus on Lula and the PT, who for over two decades have been branded by many conservatives as the ones solely responsible for rampant corruption,” said political scientist Paulo Roberto Souza of the Democracy in Check Institute, an independent research nonprofit.

articles.title: DAVID MARCUS: Peggy Flanagan's DEI record and fraud scandal put Minnesota Senate race in the spotlight
articles.summary: Peggy Flanagan's DEI record, fraud scandal, and Medicare for All stance face new scrutiny as the Minnesota Senate race tightens against Michele Tafoya.
articles.body: "The lieutenant governor [Peggy Flanagan], even as we sit here today, continues to take absolutely no accountability for any of the fraud issues, and she continues to blame the governor. And I'm going to be honest: It's pissing me off." The above quote is not from a Republican, but from Democratic Rep. Angie Craig, D-Minn, in July when she was running in the Senate primary against Peggy Flanagan. While harsh words are often lightly thrown in primary battles, in this case, one must ask: Where is the lie? While Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and Colorado’s House candidate Milot Kiros have snagged headlines for their far left views, Flanagan has been able to hide a bit. However, the tightening race in Minnesota, as shown both through on-the-ground reporting and in polling, is putting Democrats everywhere in an awkward position because they had thought Flanagan’s leftist lunacy would float under the radar this cycle. Well, not anymore. DAVID MARCUS: IN DEEP BLUE MINNESOTA A RED DAWN MAY BE RISING AHEAD OF THE MIDTERMS Now that the Gopher State is firmly in the political spotlight, voters will be reminded, for example, of Flanagan wearing a T-shirt that says "Protect Trans Kids" on it, with a picture of a large Bowie knife — which can only be rationally read as a threat of physical violence. We know what the shirt means because not just threats, but also acts of physical violence by, or in defense of, members of the trans community have become commonplace in our society. Harry Potter author J.K. Rowling is threatened constantly for simply believing that men cannot become women. Trans-related mass shootings have become a norm. Progressive protests and internet forums echo with terms like "Kill All TERFS (Trans Excluding Radical Feminists)," and instead of trying to calm tensions, Flanagan’s answer is to pour gasoline on the rhetorical fire with death threats while insisting that men belong in women’s sports. PEGGY FLANAGAN VOWS TO 'RIP ICE APART' AFTER TOPPLING MODERATE DEM IN KEY SENATE BATTLE On the economy, Flanagan also flails to the far left, favoring a $17 national minimum wage that would crush many small businesses, not just in Minnesota, but across America, and Medicare for All that would take away the private insurance of every citizen. When it comes to Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion, Flanagan is exactly where you would expect her to be, just to the left of chairman Mao, saying in 2023, "We remain committed to centering the people most impacted by disparities based on race, geography, and economic status … We will continue working to engage and empower those who have been historically left out of government." Among the farcical programs created by this unhinged rubric was Minnesota’s marijuana legalization efforts that gave loans, often forgivable, to people based on "special equity status," to open dispensaries — many of which have now failed and closed. Truly, only government leftists could foul up selling weed, something mastered by the stoners we all knew in high school. Of course, this emphasis on "special equity" and DEI also lies at the root of Flanagan’s massive Somali fraud scandal, where whistleblowers were ignored as hundreds of millions, at least, were pilfered because Peggy was uncomfortable criticizing Somalis. To make matters worse, some of the alleged fraudsters appear to be inside Flanagan’s inner circle, including Nimco Ahmed, with whom Flanagan recently appeared in full hijab, no less, whose autism center is now under federal investigation. For her part, Flanagan’s opponent, Republican Michele Tafoya, is offering Minnesotans a centrist and moderate version of the GOP with stances such as supporting abortion rights, even angering more traditional conservatives. Tafoya has taken her middle-of-the-road message on a media blitz in recent weeks. One half expects her to be interviewed on Prairie Home Companion, while Flanagan has all but been in hiding, entertaining only the most comfortable and coddling interviews possible. Notwithstanding the fact that early voting has already begun in Minnesota, a month is too long for Flanagan to pull a Biden-esque hide-in-the-basement strategy, especially as Tafoya’s national profile is only growing stronger. To date, Flanagan has not agreed to debate the eager Tafoya, presumably for all the reasons, reflecting her failed record. But at this point, refusing to take on her opponent face-to-face might play worse than any embarrassment the event itself might cause. The Democrats have a Peggy Flanagan problem. They really, really, really don’t want her and her bizarre brand of progressivism on the Sunday shows, but at this point, they may have no choice. articles.title: Give priority to drought & not SIR: Congress demands EC to extend SIR by two months in Maha
articles.summary: Congress urges Election Commission to extend Maharashtra electoral roll SIR deadline by 2 months, citing glitches, low response and worsening drought.
articles.body: Pune: State Congress has urged Election Commission of India (ECI) to extend the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls by two months, citing procedural discrepancies, poor response rates and the worsening drought situation across large parts of Maharashtra.In a letter to Chief Electoral Officer S Chockalingam on Tuesday, Maharashtra Congress president Harshwardhan Sapkal said the current deadline of Oct 12 was impractical given multiple challenges affecting the revision process.Sapkal stated in the letter that more than 1.5 crore voters had been placed in the absent, shifted, duplicate, dead and other (ASDDO) category, but only about 3.9 lakh had submitted the mandatory Form 6. “The form itself has lacunae that were brought to ECI’s notice, but no corrected forms have been printed yet. There are also issues with server connectivity that ECI should address,” Sapkal wrote.The state Congress chief also raised concerns over technical glitches, particularly server connectivity issues, which he said were hampering the exercise.Further complicating the process, Sapkal said teachers deployed as booth-level officers (BLOs) were engaged in mid-term examinations. “With the Navaratra festival set to follow, voters and election staff will struggle to complete the exercise within the existing timeline. The Oct 12 deadline is not sufficient in the present circumstances and should be extended by at least two months,” Sapkal said in the letter.The issue is expected to figure prominently at Maharashtra Pradesh Congress Committee (MPCC) meeting in Mumbai on Thursday, where party leaders will also discuss the drought situation in the state.MPCC vice-president Mohan Joshi said nearly 75% of Maharashtra was grappling with drought-like conditions, making water scarcity and relief measures a bigger priority than the voter revision drive. “With no immediate elections scheduled in the state, there is enough scope for ECI to extend the SIR deadline,” Joshi said.He said Congress planned to launch a protest against SIR, arguing that citizens were being compelled to focus on documentation requirements at a time when many regions were struggling with severe water distress. “The priority should be addressing the drought crisis rather than burdening people with the SIR process,” Joshi added.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Pune | Silver Rate in Pune | Bank Holidays in Pune | Public Holidays in Pune | Petrol Price in Pune | Diesel Price in Pune | CNG Price in Pune | LPG Price in PuneStay updated with the latest Pune news.
